evidence.label: Exact quantum factoring over a fixed finite gate set

headline: Proves polynomial-size quantum circuits over a fixed gate set factor every integer with probability exactly one.
scope: Uniform quantum circuits over one fixed finite gate set (NOT, CNOT, Toffoli, Hadamard, diag(1,i), inverses, singly controlled versions), for every integer N ≥ 2.
plain: Shor's 1994 quantum algorithm factors whole numbers quickly, but it can fail and must sometimes be rerun. This paper builds quantum circuits that output the full prime factorization of every number with probability exactly one. They use one fixed, small set of gates and stay polynomial in size. Lean checks the main theorem; the circuits are far too large to be practical.
doesNot: This does not give a practical speed-up, a classical factoring method, or circuits small enough for any foreseeable quantum computer.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Shor, polynomial-time quantum factoring with bounded error
scorecard.significanceWhy: It removes the failure probability from quantum factoring while keeping one fixed finite gate set and polynomial worst-case size.

explanation:
Factor N = 15 the quantum way. Pick a = 7 and look at its powers modulo 15. They run 7, 4, 13, 1, so the order of 7 is r = 4. The order is the least power that gives 1. Half the order gives 7² ≡ 4, a square root of 1 that is not ±1. Then gcd(4 − 1, 15) = 3 and gcd(4 + 1, 15) = 5. So 15 = 3 × 5.

Shor's algorithm finds orders quickly with a quantum computer. It factors in polynomial time with bounded error[10]. Bounded error means each run can fail with some small chance. Checking a proposed answer makes reruns reliable. But a procedure that retries until success need not have a polynomial worst-case running time[2]. Exact versions existed only in stronger models. Mosca's exact algorithm allowed gate settings computed during the run[3]. The obstacle with a fixed gate set is that rotations by arbitrary angles cannot be built exactly. Approximating them ever more finely does not give probability-one answers[11].

The paper proves a uniform family of polynomial-size quantum circuits[1]. Uniform means an ordinary computer can write out each circuit in polynomial time. The circuits output the complete prime factorization of every N ≥ 2 with probability one[1]. One fixed finite gate set suffices: NOT, CNOT, Toffoli, Hadamard, diag(1, i), their inverses and singly controlled versions[8]. The gate and qubit counts are bounded by a fixed polynomial in the bit length of N[9].

The key trick ends with amplitude amplification, a step that boosts the chance of a good outcome. Suppose a good outcome has probability exactly 1/4. Write this as sin²θ = 1/4, so θ = 30°. One amplification step turns the probability into sin²(3θ) = sin²(90°) = 1. So the whole difficulty is making the success probability exactly 1/4[4]. The paper does this with dyadic numbers, fractions whose denominators are powers of two. Its order trial hits the true order with an exact dyadic probability[5]. Along the way, each run also factors p − 1 for its primes p, recursively. A deterministic primality test, adapted from Agrawal, Kayal and Saxena, checks the prime labels[6].

The constructions are not meant to save resources. Their large polynomial sizes are not offered as practical improvements[7]. The paper makes no claim of a classical polynomial-time factoring algorithm[12].

How sure is this? Lean, a computer proof checker, has a formal proof of the main theorem. It covers the uniform polynomial-size circuit family, the fixed gate set and the exact probability one. No specialist review of the paper has been published.
hypeCheck: Solid. Lean covers the main theorem; the circuits are polynomial but very large and are not a practical improvement. No specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: For a modulo m, the least positive r with a^r ≡ 1 (mod m).
Each run is right with probability at least some fixed amount, such as 2/3, but may fail.
The fixed list of basic operations a quantum circuit is allowed to use.
One circuit for each input length, all written out by a single efficient ordinary program.
A quantum step that raises the probability of a marked outcome, generalizing Grover's search.
A fraction whose denominator is a power of two, such as 3/8.
The number of gates and qubits grows at most like a fixed power of the number of input digits.
